title: The grave

segments.voice: Yesterday, mawt, death, and your line: return. The soul at peace was called back to its Lord. Did you do one thing you'd want done before going home? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-four.

Two seas, loosed by their Lord, run up against each other and meet. Water against water. The Qur'an, in Surah ar-Rahman, says of them, in Pickthall's words: "There is a barrier between them. They encroach not." The Arabic word for that barrier is barzakh. Hold on to it, because the same word turns up somewhere much quieter. Not at the shoreline. At the graveside. Today, the barrier that stands between this life and the Day.
screen: `TWO SEAS, SIDE BY SIDE.` → `A BARRIER BETWEEN THEM.` → `THE SAME WORD, AT THE GRAVE.`

segments.voice: In Surah al-Mu'minun, someone at the point of death begs to be sent back, to do the good they left undone. The answer is no, and then a phrase, Pickthall again: "and behind them is a barrier until the day when they are raised." Barzakh. So the word that holds two seas apart also names the stretch between dying and rising. Not this world any more, not yet the Day. The in-between. It is also spoken of as the grave, al-qabr, though the barzakh is more than a hole in the ground. What happens there? The Qur'an says little in detail, and the hadith say more. One in Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Ibn 'Umar, says that when a person dies, their place in the next life is shown to them morning and evening, and they are told: this is your place, until Allah raises you. So the in-between is not empty waiting. It is waiting with a view. Scholars have discussed how to speak of it, since it is part of the unseen, al-ghayb, and they are careful to say the hadith describe it without explaining how. And notice what this does to a graveyard. A hadith in Sahih Muslim has the Prophet, peace be upon him, going out to the graveyard of al-Baqi' in Medina at night and greeting the dead with peace, and asking forgiveness for them. He greets them because, in this teaching, the people in those graves are not gone. They are across a barrier. Like the two seas, close, side by side, and kept apart.
screen: `SEND ME BACK. THE ANSWER IS NO.` · `A BARRIER UNTIL THE DAY OF RAISING.` · `WAITING, WITH A VIEW.` · then, large: `GREETING THE ONES ACROSS THE BARRIER.`

segments.voice: The practice for this week is to visit a graveyard, when you can: a family grave, a town cemetery, any quiet place where people are buried. Walk slowly and read a few names. For now, settle and breathe. Bring to mind one person who has died, someone you knew, or someone whose name you only heard. Think of them not as gone, but as across a barrier. If you pray, you can greet them as the Prophet greeted the dead at al-Baqi', with peace, and ask forgiveness for them. If not, simply say their name once, and wish them well. The bell holds the time.
Barzakh. A barrier; in Muslim teaching, the in-between of the grave, from death until the Day of rising. Today's word.

Your line: the in-between. Today, when you pass a cemetery, or hear a name of someone who's died, pause one second and greet them. Tomorrow, the questions asked in the grave. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: Muslims visit graves to remember the hereafter, greet the dead with salam, and ask forgiveness for them; the time between death and the Day of Resurrection is called the barzakh, or the life of the grave.
